query: Starting from crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals, what single intervention could overcome the unresolved risk of instability during operation in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime? Although many physical and chemical fabrication methods have been developed, synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly understood, limiting assessment of these materials for high-temperature applications. The hypothesis should remain compatible with a multielement solid solution and the potential for catalytic performance at low noble-metal content. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to untreated nanoparticles, the application and compositional boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment with a clear failure criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Supporting high-entropy alloy nanoparticles on a stable, high-surface-area material can overcome the risk of instability during operation in the 773-1173 K catalytic regime.
generation.material_initial_state: Crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals
generation.intervention: Supporting the nanoparticles on a stable, high-surface-area material
generation.conditions: Operation in the 773-1173 K catalytic regime
generation.mechanism: The support material stabilizes the nanoparticles, preventing sintering and aggregation, and maintains their high surface area, thereby preserving their catalytic activity
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved stability and catalytic performance of the high-entropy alloy nanoparticles
generation.boundary: Compositional boundary: near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals; Application boundary: catalytic applications in the 773-1173 K regime
generation.uncertainty: The optimal support material and its interaction with the high-entropy alloy nanoparticles are not well understood and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the catalytic performance of supported and unsupported high-entropy alloy nanoparticles in the 773-1173 K regime
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the supported nanoparticles do not exhibit improved stability and catalytic performance compared to the unsupported nanoparticles, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: We have developed advanced ammonia decomposition catalysts based on high-entropy alloys made of earth-abundant elements. The HEA CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles enabled robust tuning of the Co/Mo ratio and breaking the miscibility limitation in conventional bimetallic Co-Mo catalysts. These novel catalysts achieved significantly enhanced catalytic activities and stabilities, with the improvement factors exceeding 20 times as compared to precious metal Ru, and even more so versus conventional Co-Mo catalysts. Their catalytic activities and kinetics were further found to exhibit a volcano-type behavior independent of the Co/Mo ratio, which was successfully interpreted by using the nitrogen adsorption energy as the descriptor and a mixed surface site mechanism derived from atomistic modeling. The robust tunability of alloy composition and surface adsorption property demonstrated on the HEA catalysts indicate great potential for their implementation in practical reactors with the catalytic performance optimized under various reaction conditions.

High-entropy alloys, containing five or even more metals, have attracted significant attentions, because of their unique chemical and physical complexity, which endow alloys with tunable features and properties such as thermal stability, superior corrosion resistance, high hardness, exceptional ductility, and superparamagnetism. A wide range of researches have revealed that the nanoparticles loading on the supports could significantly improve specific surface area and surface energy compared with the bulk materials or the nanoparticles themselves,. In addition, in industrial applications, the nanoparticles need to be dispersedly immobilized on granular supports, such as Al2O3, zeolite, and carbon materials etc., which can make the catalysts feature with tunable size, shape, and stability, enhancing the catalytic performance. Therefore, the supported high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) can be promisingly applied in catalysis, chemical sensing, biology, and energy conversion. However, the common extreme high temperature related approaches such as arc melting and laser cladding are not suitable for supporting HEA-NPs due to the rapid growth and aggregation of nanoparticles.
